title: Advanced Python: ML, Django & Automation
intro: This term your Python grows up: you will crunch numbers with NumPy and SciPy, teach a computer to guess prices with scikit-learn, and put it all on the web with Django. You will finish by building robots that do boring jobs for real people.
termProject: Ogun Crop-Price Helper: a scikit-learn tomato-price predictor trained on clearly labelled practice data, a Django dashboard of real prices learners collect from Ilaro, Owode and Sango markets, and a morning automation script that writes a dollar-rate price note for a local shop.

weeks.title: NumPy: A Whole Market in One Line
weeks.goal: I can store a week of market prices in a NumPy array and find the average, highest and lowest in one line each.
weeks.learn: A NumPy array is a fast row of numbers that Python can work on all at once. Instead of a loop that visits every price one by one, you write prices * 1.10 and every price changes together. Think of a market woman who raises the price of every tomato basket on her table with one shout, instead of walking to each basket. NumPy also has ready tools like mean(), max() and argmax() that tell you the answer and where it is.

research.q: Ask a trader or your parent: how much was a basket (or a paint bucket) of tomatoes on two different days this week?
research.tip: Write the two prices and the days. Real prices make your array feel alive, and you will see how fast prices move.

build.task: Put six days of tomato prices in a NumPy array and print the average, the costliest day and the price with transport added.
steps: Open a terminal and run: pip install numpy
Create a file market.py and type the code
Swap the practice prices for the ones you collected
Run python market.py and read each line out loud
build.code:
import numpy as np

# PRACTICE prices (naira) for a basket of tomatoes, Mon-Sat - change to real ones you collect
prices = np.array([4500, 4800, 5200, 5000, 6100, 5900])
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat"]

print("Average price:", round(prices.mean()))
print("Highest:", prices.max(), "on", days[prices.argmax()])
print("Lowest:", prices.min(), "on", days[prices.argmin()])

# Add 10% transport cost to EVERY price at once - no loop needed
with_transport = (prices * 1.10).round()
print("With transport:", with_transport)

# Which days were above average? (True/False for each day)
above = prices > prices.mean()
print("Above-average days:", [d for d, a in zip(days, above) if a])

weeks.title: SciPy: Does Rain Grow More Maize?
weeks.goal: I can use SciPy to find the straight-line link between two sets of numbers and use it to make a careful guess.
weeks.learn: SciPy sits on top of NumPy and gives scientists ready-made tools for statistics, curves and more. linregress draws the best straight line through your points and tells you the slope: how much one thing goes up when the other goes up. It is like a farmer who notices that every extra rainy week brings a few more bags of maize. The r value tells you how strong the link is: close to 1 is strong, close to 0 is weak. A link is a clue, not a proof.

research.q: Ask a farmer or an elder who farms: in a good rainy season, how many bags of maize or cassava do you get compared to a dry one?
research.tip: Write the two numbers and what they said about rain. It tells you if rain really matters in your area.

build.task: Use SciPy linregress on practice rain and maize numbers, then guess the harvest for 9 rainy days.
steps: Run: pip install scipy
Type the code into harvest.py
Run it and read the slope and r value
Change one maize number a lot and run again: what happens to r?
build.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# PRACTICE DATA (made up for learning): rainy days in a month vs bags of maize harvested
rain_days = np.array([3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15])
maize_bags = np.array([20, 27, 33, 42, 45, 56])

line = stats.linregress(rain_days, maize_bags)
print("Each extra rainy day adds about", round(line.slope, 2), "bags")
print("Starting point (intercept):", round(line.intercept, 2))
print("How strong is the link (r):", round(line.rvalue, 3))

guess = line.slope * 9 + line.intercept
print("Careful guess for 9 rainy days:", round(guess), "bags")

summary = stats.describe(maize_bags)
print("Average bags:", round(summary.mean, 1), "| spread (variance):", round(summary.variance, 1))

weeks.title: scikit-learn: Teach Python to Guess Tomato Prices
weeks.goal: I can train a small machine learning model on labelled practice data, test it on rows it has never seen, and make a prediction.
weeks.learn: Machine learning means showing the computer many examples so it learns a pattern by itself. In scikit-learn you give it X (the clues, like rainy days and festive season) and y (the answer, like price), then call fit() to learn and predict() to guess. It is like an apprentice at the market who watches the madam for months until she can price tomatoes alone. We always hide some rows during learning and test on them, so we know the model is not just memorising.

research.q: Ask a tomato seller: in which months is tomato cheapest and in which months is it most costly? Why?
research.tip: Write the months and the reason. This is real 'domain knowledge' that tells you which clues (X) your model needs.

build.task: Train a LinearRegression model on 6 months of practice data, test it on 2 hidden months, and predict a festive month.
steps: Run: pip install scikit-learn
Type the code into predictor.py
Run it and compare each guess with the real number
Write one sentence: is the model good enough for a trader to trust?
build.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# PRACTICE DATA (made up for learning, NOT real market prices)
# X = [rainy days that month, festive month? 1=yes 0=no]   y = basket of tomatoes (naira)
X = [[0, 1], [2, 0], [5, 0], [8, 0], [12, 0], [15, 0], [3, 1], [10, 0]]
y = [10400, 8300, 7600, 6500, 5300, 4400, 9600, 5800]

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X[:6], y[:6])            # learn from the first 6 months only

print("Testing on 2 months the model never saw:")
for clues, real in zip(X[6:], y[6:]):
    guess = model.predict([clues])[0]
    print("  Clues", clues, "guess N", round(guess), "| real N", real)

december = [[6, 1]]                 # 6 rainy days, festive season
print("Prediction for a festive month with 6 rainy days: N", round(model.predict(december)[0]))

weeks.title: Django Says Hello: Meet M-V-T
weeks.goal: I can start a Django project, explain Model-View-Template, and show my first page in the browser.
weeks.learn: Django is a Python framework for building big websites fast, used by real companies. It splits the work into three parts: the Model (the data), the View (the brain that decides what to send back) and the Template (the page people see). urls.py is the gateman: when a visitor knocks on a web address, it sends them to the right view. Think of a buka: the store room is the Model, the cook is the View, and the plate of food on your table is the Template.

research.q: Ask a trader or a farmer: if there was a website showing today's prices in nearby markets, what is the ONE thing you would want to see first?
research.tip: Write their answer word for word. It becomes the first thing your Django home page shows.

weeks.title: Django Models: A Price Book That Never Gets Lost
weeks.goal: I can build a Django model for crop prices, add it to the admin page, and save real prices into the database.
weeks.learn: A model is a Python class that describes one kind of record, like a row in a price book. Each field (crop, market, price, date) becomes a column in the database. Django's migrate command builds the database table for you, so you never write the table by hand. The admin page is a free back office where you can add, edit and delete records. It is like the madam's exercise book of prices, but it cannot get wet or torn.

research.q: Ask two traders or buyers: what are the prices of the same crop (e.g. garri or yam) in two different markets this week?
research.tip: Write crop, market, price and date for each. These become your first real records in the admin.

build.task: Make a CropPrice model, register it in the admin, and add at least three prices you collected.
steps: Paste the model into prices/models.py and the admin lines into prices/admin.py

build.code:
# ---- prices/models.py  (M = Model: the shape of our data) ----
from django.db import models

class CropPrice(models.Model):
    crop = models.CharField(max_length=50)
    market = models.CharField(max_length=50)
    price = models.PositiveIntegerField(help_text="Price in naira")
    date = models.DateField()

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.crop} at {self.market}: N{self.price}"

# ---- prices/admin.py ----
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import CropPrice

admin.site.register(CropPrice)

# ---- naijamarket/settings.py: add "prices" inside INSTALLED_APPS ----
# Terminal:
#   python manage.py makemigrations
#   python manage.py migrate
#   python manage.py createsuperuser
#   python manage.py runserver      then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/

weeks.title: Scalable Apps: Build for One Shop, Ready for a Thousand
weeks.goal: I can organise code into small functions with one settings dictionary, and use caching so repeated questions are answered instantly.
weeks.learn: A scalable app keeps working well when users grow from 10 to 10,000. Two habits help: put settings in one place so you change them once, and do not repeat slow work. A cache remembers answers to questions it has already been asked. It is like a POS agent who memorises today's charges after the first customer, instead of calling the boss every time. Python's lru_cache adds this memory to a function in one line.

weeks.title: Big Data, Small Memory: Generators
weeks.goal: I can use a generator to process 100,000 rows one at a time without filling the computer's memory.
weeks.learn: When data is huge, loading it all at once can freeze a small laptop. A generator uses yield to hand over one item at a time, like a bread seller who brings loaves out of the oven one tray at a time instead of piling the whole day's bread on the table. Your loop works the same way, but memory stays small. Big websites do the same with pagination: they show 20 results per page, not one million.

weeks.title: Automation: Let Python Tidy the Mess
weeks.goal: I can write a script that automatically sorts a messy folder of files into neat folders by type.
weeks.learn: Automation means giving boring, repeated jobs to the computer. Python's pathlib can see every file in a folder and its type (.jpg, .docx), and shutil can move it. A rule chooses the right folder for each file, and a loop repeats it for every file. It is like a sorting boy at the depot who puts every parcel on the right bus - he never gets tired and never complains.

research.q: Ask a teacher, a secretary or a business owner: what boring computer or phone task do you repeat every week?
research.tip: Write the task and how long it takes. The best automation scripts solve a real person's weekly headache.

build.task: Write a script that creates practice files and sorts them into Pictures, Documents, Spreadsheets and Others.
steps: Type the code into tidy.py in an empty practice folder (never your real files)
Run it and open the class_work folder
Add a rule so .mp3 files go to a 'Music' folder

build.code:
from pathlib import Path
import shutil

# PRACTICE ONLY: we create fake empty files so no real work is touched
folder = Path("class_work")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name in ["essay.docx", "farm.jpg", "scores.xlsx", "song.mp3", "jollof.jpg"]:
    (folder / name).touch()

groups = {".jpg": "Pictures", ".docx": "Documents", ".xlsx": "Spreadsheets"}

for file in list(folder.iterdir()):
    if file.is_file():                                     # skip folders
        target = groups.get(file.suffix.lower(), "Others")   # the rule
        (folder / target).mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        shutil.move(str(file), str(folder / target / file.name))
        print("Moved", file.name, "->", target)

weeks.title: Project: The Morning Price Note Robot
weeks.goal: I can write an automation script that fetches today's dollar-naira rate from a free API and writes a ready price note for a shop.
weeks.learn: Many Nigerian shop prices move with the dollar, so shop owners check the rate every morning. Our script asks a free public API (open.er-api.com, no key needed) for today's rate, works out naira costs, and saves a neat note to a file. A scheduler (cron on Linux, Task Scheduler on Windows) is the trigger that can run it every morning by itself. It is like a newspaper vendor who drops the paper at your gate at 7am without being asked.

research.q: Ask a shop owner who sells imported goods: how do you decide when to change your prices?
research.tip: Write what they check and how often. Your robot should give them exactly that information, in their words.

build.task: Build a script that fetches today's USD-NGN rate and writes price_note.txt for a provision shop.
steps: Type the code into price_robot.py (needs internet)
Change the practice USD costs to items from your research
Run it and open price_note.txt
Bonus: ask your trainer to help schedule it for 7am
build.code:
import json, urllib.request
from datetime import date

URL = "https://open.er-api.com/v6/latest/USD"     # free public API, no key needed

try:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(URL, timeout=10) as reply:
        naira = json.load(reply)["rates"]["NGN"]
except Exception as e:
    raise SystemExit(f"No internet or API problem: {e}")

items = {"Imported rice (50kg bag)": 75, "Tin tomato (carton)": 18}   # PRACTICE USD costs

lines = [f"Shop price note for {date.today()}", f"1 USD = N{naira:,.2f}"]
for item, usd in items.items():
    lines.append(f"{item}: about N{usd * naira:,.0f}")

with open("price_note.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(lines))
print("\n".join(lines))
# Schedule it: Linux cron  0 7 * * *  python3 price_robot.py   (or Windows Task Scheduler)

weeks.say: My robot fetches today's dollar rate from a free API and writes a price note, and a scheduler can run it every morning.

trainer.open: Shop owners wake up and check the dollar. Today you build a robot that does it for them before they open the shop.
plan: Ask: who in your research checks the dollar rate? How?
Walk through the API JSON in a browser: find rates then NGN
Pairs run the robot and edit the items from their research
Show the note; trainer demonstrates a cron or Task Scheduler entry
props: Internet connection (or a saved sample JSON reply as backup)
A printed price list from a provision shop
lookfor: Finds the NGN value in the API reply on their own
Explains what happens with no internet
Adapts items and wording to their research shop owner
fix: Gets KeyError because they typed rates['ngn'] in small letters
JSON keys are exact - open the API in the browser and copy the key as it appears
Presents the practice USD costs as real prices
Remind them to label practice numbers, or collect real costs from the shop owner first
